title: Versioning: knowing what you have and what changed
promise: You'll put a number and a date on what works, and keep a change list that still makes sense in six months. By the end you'll have your version 1.0 marked and you'll be able to explain in one sentence what changed since the previous one.
why: Nuria passed her query system to a colleague at another practice so she could set up the same thing. Three weeks later the colleague wrote: «this answers differently from yours». Nuria had no way of knowing whether it was the same setup, whether documents were missing, or whether she herself had changed the instructions in between. There were no versions, no dates, no change list. She had to compare the two configurations by hand, screen against screen, for a whole afternoon, only to discover she'd changed one line of the instructions in August and forgotten.

theory.title: Without a version you can't talk about what you have
theory.text: While you're working alone on one thing, you can live without versions. In the moment there's a second person, a second setup or a second month, the question you can't answer appears: is what I have running the same as what I had in June? And out of that come all the impossible conversations of the «it worked for me» kind. Putting a version on something is giving a name to a specific state of your setup so you can refer to it. It isn't bureaucracy: it's being able to say «on 1.2 this worked» and have that sentence mean something.
theory.analogy: It's the number plate on a car. Without it, «my car» and «your car» are the same phrase and there's no way to know which one the mechanic means.
theory.example: Nuria spent an afternoon comparing screens for want of one line saying «1.2 - 14 August - changed the contradiction rule».

theory.title: Three numbers and what each one means
theory.text: The standard form is three numbers separated by dots, like 1.4.2, and it works simply. The first changes when something breaks for whoever was using it: you change how you get in, you remove a feature, you change the output format. The second, when you add something new that breaks nothing that came before. And the third, when you only fix a fault. You don't have to be a purist: what it buys you is that whoever sees the number knows whether they can update calmly or whether something is about to change for them. If it feels like too much, use two numbers and be done. What matters isn't which system, it's that there is one.
theory.example: 1.0.0: the system as you left it on day one. 1.1.0: you added the date warning. 1.1.1: you fixed a typo in the instructions. 2.0.0: you changed the answer format, and anyone using it needs to know.

theory.title: The change list is written for someone else, not for you
theory.text: A useful change list doesn't say «updated the instructions». It says what changed from the point of view of whoever uses it: «it now warns you when the document is more than two years old». The difference is that the first is no use to you in six months and the second is. Three lines per version is enough: the date, what changed in plain language, and why. The «why» is the one you appreciate most later, when you're about to undo a change and can't remember what problem it solved.
theory.example: «1.1.0 - 14 Aug 2026. It now warns you if the document the fact comes from is more than two years old. Reason: I sent an expired surcharge to a client.»

theory.title: Marking is different from saving
theory.text: In lesson 37 you made copies so you could go back. Marking a version is a different thing: it's pointing at one of those copies and saying «this is the good one, the one in use». You save many times a day; you mark a version rarely, when something reaches a state you want to be able to recover and name. The practical difference is that copies are for you and for emergencies, and versions are for talking to other people and for knowing what's running right now.
theory.example: Álvaro saves every time he touches anything, several times a day, and those copies expire on their own: only the last few matter to him. He marks a version once a month, or when he changes something his patients will notice. When someone asks what he has running, he answers with the version; when something breaks, he reaches for the copy.

theory.title: Writing down what's in use right now
theory.text: There's a one-screen file almost nobody has that solves half the confusion: the one saying which version is running right now, where, since when and who uses it. When you have one setup on your computer, another you handed to someone, and a half-finished one you were testing, that file is the only thing telling the three apart. And if anyone else ever has to get involved, it's the first thing they'll look for.
theory.example: «IN USE: v1.2, since 14 August, on the practice's n8n account. Nuria uses it and her colleague's copy is v1.0, without the date warning.»

theory.title: When to bump the version and when not to
theory.text: You don't have to mark a version for every little thing you touch: that turns the list into noise. The practical rule is to mark when one of three things happens. One, that someone else is using it and something is about to change for them. Two, that you've fixed something that had caused you grief and you want to be able to point at when it was resolved. And three, that you're about to make a big change and you want the previous state nailed down before you start. Outside those three cases, save a copy and carry on working.
theory.example: Nuria marks a version when she changes the instructions or when a big batch of documents goes in. Day-to-day tweaks don't bump the version.

tasks.title: Mark your version 1.0
tasks.action: Take what you have running right now, exactly as it is. Create a folder called «v1.0» inside your copies folder and put in it everything from the list in lesson 37: exported workflows, instructions, prompts, configuration screenshots. This is your official starting point.
tasks.expect: A «v1.0» folder with everything in it. From now on you can say «the 1.0» and have it mean something concrete.
tasks.stuck: If your setup isn't finished, mark it anyway. 1.0 doesn't mean perfect, it means «this is what there is today». That's far more useful than waiting until it's done, because it never will be.

tasks.title: Start the change list
tasks.action: Create the file and write the first entry for your 1.0 with three parts: the version and the date, what the setup does in two sentences, and what it's known not to do yet. That third part, the known limits, is the one anyone picking this up later will appreciate most, yourself included.
tasks.expect: One entry. Format: «v1.0 - [date]. What it does: … What it doesn't do yet: …»
tasks.stuck: If you don't know what to put under «what it doesn't do», pull from the «what-its-for.txt» file from lesson 34 and the checks from lesson 35. Your limits are already written there.

tasks.title: Make a change and bump the version properly
tasks.where: In your setup and in your two files
tasks.action: Make a real change you had outstanding, however small. When it works and you've run the checklist, do three things: create the new version's folder with everything in it, write the entry in «changes.txt» explaining what changes for whoever uses it and why, and decide the number using the three rules from the theory.
tasks.expect: A «v1.1» folder and a new entry. Read the entry aloud: if someone who doesn't know your setup wouldn't understand what changed for them, rewrite it.
tasks.stuck: If you're torn between bumping the second or the third number, ask yourself whether you added something (second) or only fixed something that should already have worked (third). And if you get it wrong, never mind: what matters is that there's a dated entry.

tasks.title: Write down what's in use right now
tasks.action: Four lines: which version is running, where exactly (which account, which tool, which folder), since when, and who else uses it if anyone does. Put it in the most visible place in your working folder.
tasks.expect: Four lines. If you have copies in other people's hands, note which version each of them has: that's exactly the fact Nuria was missing.
tasks.stuck: If you have three half-finished setups and don't know which is in use, that confusion is exactly the problem this file solves. Go to the tool and see which one is activated: that's the one.

tasks.title: Have the AI write the list for someone else
tasks.action: If you're going to hand the setup to someone, or simply to keep it tidy, give it your raw change notes and ask it to rewrite them from the user's point of view.
tasks.prompt:
I have change notes for a setup of mine, written for myself and rough. I want to turn them into a change list that someone who uses the setup but didn't build it would understand.

MY NOTES:
[PASTE YOUR NOTES]

RULES:
1. Each entry from the point of view of whoever uses it: what they notice, not what I touched inside.
2. Two lines per version at most.
3. Clearly flag the ones that force them to change how they use it.
4. If a note of mine is so vague it can't be translated, don't invent it: put it aside with a specific question for me.

No introduction and no summary. Just the list.
tasks.expect: A clean list and possibly a separate list of things you need to clarify. That second list is useful: those are the changes you noted badly at the time.
tasks.stuck: If it rewrites everything in marketing language like «experience improvements», say: «Drop the adjectives. Say exactly what it does differently now, with the name of the screen or the field.»

tasks.title: Close the block by reviewing the five files
tasks.action: By this point you should have five files from the block: checks, breakdowns, going-back, changes and in-use. Open them all, check each has real content and not an empty template, and put today's date at the end. If any is missing, complete it now: it's fifteen minutes and it's the difference between a personal setup and one you can defend.
tasks.expect: Five files with content and a date. This folder is what you show when someone asks whether your setup is reliable, and it's half of what gets assessed when you defend your final project.
tasks.stuck: If one is empty because you didn't see the point, reread what it was for in its lesson. The one most often left blank is the breakdown log, and it's precisely the one that saves the most time three months in.

matters: That without a version you can't talk about what you have running or compare it with before.
That the change list is written from what the user notices, not from what you touched inside.
That saving a copy and marking a version are different things: one is for emergencies, the other for talking.
That the «why» behind each change is what stops you undoing something that solved a problem.
ignore: Being a purist about the three numbers. Having a system matters more than which one.
Version management tools. Dated folders and a text file are plenty.
Marking a version for every tweak. You mark when one of the three things happens.
canDo: Say which version you have running and since when.
Explain in one sentence what changed between two versions.
Know which version each person you handed it to has.
Have your setup documented in five files that read in five minutes.
cantDo: Recover versions from before today if you didn't save them.
Know what changed if you didn't note it at the time.
Stop someone using an old version: you can only know which they have.
Replace testing. Versioning doesn't say whether it works, it says what's in place.
words: The name you give a specific state of your setup so you can refer to it.
What changed in each version, told from what the user notices.
The kind that forces the user to change how they use it. It bumps the first number.
Pointing at one copy as the good one and naming it. Different from saving.
Which version is running right now and where. The fact missing from almost every setup.
next: Block closed: you know how to check, read errors, go back, keep watch and version. The next block is about what can genuinely hurt you even when everything works: the keys, other people's data, and the invoice at the end of the month.
